rationale: A wins because it respects the load-bearing facts and turns missing proof into guardrails instead of decoration. Its line that "no price change at retail covers grocery shelves, not café menus" is exactly the caveat that keeps a reporter from puncturing the pitch. B has usable bones, but "customers who don't specify get oat milk" converts a default non-dairy option into a default milk order; that is how a pitch becomes a correction.
gaps_in_A: "Plant-based dairy's growth era is over" is stronger than the supplied facts. A admits it needs category data, but the headline still makes the unsupported sector-wide claim.

"Oatly is closing a plant and cutting its carbon footprint in the same quarter" depends on timing the update does not precisely establish. Say the events are concurrent only if the announcement dates prove it.

"defaults quietly decide what thousands of customers drink every day" slightly blurs default non-dairy option with default drink behavior. It needs tighter wording so it does not imply all unspecified milk orders become oat milk.
gaps_in_B: "customers who don't specify get oat milk" is not in the update and is likely wrong. The fact says default non-dairy option, not default milk for every order.
"falling volumes, shrinking retail shelf space, canceled expansions" invents category context. If you need those facts, source them; don't smuggle them into the angle.
"Customer-story (the coffee chain's procurement decision) — no_journalist_shape" contradicts the kept lead angle, which is also the coffee chain's menu/procurement decision. Pick a lane.

"one of its larger US distribution wins" and "new formula for profitability" turn a partnership plus plant closure into a strategy without an on-record link. That may be the story, but it is not yet a fact.
